summary.text: Viral replication is the formation of new viruses inside the target host cells during infection.
A virus attaches to a host cell, passes into it, has its protein coat removed, and then rapidly produces copies of its genome.
The host cell has to supply the energy, the synthetic machinery and the precursors for making viral proteins and nucleic acids.

facts.label: DNA virus site
facts.value: Most DNA viruses assemble in the nucleus

facts.label: RNA virus site
facts.value: Most RNA viruses develop solely in the cytoplasm

facts.label: Common way in
facts.value: Receptor-mediated endocytosis, at no energy cost to the virus

facts.label: Rhinovirus attachment
facts.value: It binds ICAM-1, a receptor that normally helps cells adhere

facts.label: Two life cycles
facts.value: The lytic cycle and the lysogenic cycle

items.prompt: A lab puts virus particles in a flask of nutrient broth with no living cells. Will they multiply there?

options.label: Yes, the broth supplies what they need to copy themselves
No, because viruses multiply only in living cells
Yes, but only at a slower rate than usual
Only if the broth is warmed above room temperature

items.explain: Viruses multiply only in living cells; the host cell provides the energy, machinery and precursors.

items.prompt: What lets a virus stick to the right cell before it gets in?

options.label: Hooks of lipid that pierce straight through the cell
The cell's own digestive enzymes, which pull it close
A protein extending from its capsid that binds a receptor on the cell surface
A sticky film that lets it cling to any surface

items.explain: Attachment is often achieved by a virus attachment protein extending from the capsid that binds a surface receptor on the host cell.

items.prompt: Rhinovirus binds ICAM-1, a receptor that cells use to stick to each other. What does this show?

options.label: Viruses build their own receptors on host cells
Cells make receptors that are meant to welcome viruses
Receptors only work on virus-infected cells
Viruses can exploit normal cell receptor functions to attach

items.explain: Viruses can exploit normal cell receptor functions by mimicking molecules that bind to host cell receptors.

items.prompt: When a virus slips in by the most common route, which side spends energy on the entry?

options.label: Only the cell being infected
Only the virus
Both share the cost equally
Neither, since it needs no energy at all

items.explain: Receptor-mediated endocytosis comes at no energy cost to the virus, only the host cell.

items.prompt: A virus is inside a cell with its genetic material still packaged. Which step must come before its genome can be copied?

options.label: Attachment to a receptor on the plasma membrane
Uncoating, which removes the virion's coat and frees the genes
Cell-to-cell fusion that forms a syncytium
Entry through the cell's outer membrane

items.explain: Uncoating is the third step, after attachment and entry, and comes before replication of the genome.

items.prompt: A viral genome is built into the host's genome, copied whenever the host divides, and only later triggered to make virus. Which life cycle is this?

options.label: The lysogenic cycle, where the viral genome joins the host's
The lytic cycle, where the virus hijacks machinery at once
Cell-to-cell fusion, where infected cells draw in neighbours
Endocytosis, where the cell wraps a virus in a vesicle

items.explain: In the lysogenic cycle the viral genome is incorporated into the host genome and copied with it, and can later be triggered to begin viral production.
